card.hook: The Red Fort's walls are so red that the sky looks a bit pale next to them, and the Lahori Gate is where that colour really hits you. It's the fort's most photographed spot, and you don't need a ticket for it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the approach road right in front of the Lahori Gate, the fort's main entrance, and face the gate. The sandstone gateway rises in front of you with a bastion on each side, and the fort's walls stretch away to the east behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x if you're close and want the full height of the gate and both bastions. Step back and use 1x for a more natural look, or try 2x to pick out the stonework and the top of the gateway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the walls level, then tap the red stone and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the sandstone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour, when the low light warms the red stone. Take a few frames in a row and keep the sharpest.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Lahori Gate with the red sandstone walls behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more gate in, and tilt the phone up a little so the gateway rises over your shoulder. Golden-hour light makes the walls glow behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back near the main gates on the Lahori Gate side while you stand in front of the gate, so the photo takes in the fort's full height.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography for personal use is permitted, but there are no drones, and no flash inside some buildings. Don't climb on anything for a shot. Access in front of the fort may be closed at sunset and restricted on 15 August, so check the official site on the day.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the gate fits top to bottom with a strip of sky above it, and the walls are dead straight on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Shah Jahan had the fort built after moving his capital from Agra to Delhi, and it was finished in 1648. The design is credited to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who also worked on the Taj Mahal. On 15 August 1947 Jawaharlal Nehru raised the Indian flag above the Lahori Gate, and the Prime Minister still raises the flag there every Independence Day.

card.hook: Rickshaws, tangled wires, a thousand signs and a few thousand people, and then the Red Fort's walls quietly closing off the far end like a full stop. It's loud and messy, and it's the reason the photo works.
card.stand_here: Stand on Chandni Chowk, in the middle of the road, and face east towards the Red Fort end. Let the road lead your eye straight into the picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the street. If it feels too tight, drop to zoom 0.5x, or try zoom 2x to pull the Red Fort a little closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fort at the far end, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, and the light is gentler looking down the street. Later the market fills up, and the crowds become part of the picture.
card.selfie_here: Try Ghantaghar, the old clock-tower spot in the middle of the market near the Town Hall on Rai Kedarnath Marg. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the street behind your shoulder. It's a sensible central spot rather than an official selfie spot. Fountain Chowk, opposite Gurdwara Sisganj, is a second option, with the Victorian fountain beside you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone in your hand or on a wrist strap in the crush. Watch for rickshaws and other traffic, and take a few quick frames rather than stopping in the flow of people. The Red Fort at the far end is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Wait for a rickshaw or a walker to drift into the lower third of your frame, then grab it. Bonus points if the fort is still sitting neatly at the end of the road.
card.good_to_know: Chandni Chowk means "Moonlight Square". The market was laid out in 1650 under Shah Jahan, and his daughter Jahanara is credited with the design. It began with about 1,560 shops and a water channel down the middle, and the centre of the market is still called Ghantaghar.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Chandni Chowk, in the middle of the road, and face east towards the Red Fort end. Let the road lead your eye straight into the picture.

card.hook: Picture a straight green avenue with one huge stone arch waiting at the end of it. Everything around India Gate is symmetrical, so even a quick snap looks planned.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kartavya Path, at the India Gate end of the boulevard. Face east, because the arch is straight along the avenue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the arch and the avenue fit in one frame. Tap 2x to bring the arch a little closer without moving. When you turn round to look back west along the avenue, try 0.5x to fit it all in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the arch on the centre line and keep your phone level so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go at dawn or blue hour, when the light is soft. It's also quieter than the busy middle of the day, and holidays are the busiest of all.
card.selfie_here: Try the Kartavya Path boulevard: face away from the gate with the arch over your shoulder, using the front camera (or 0.5x if you want more of the avenue in). For a closer shot, stand beside the Amar Jawan Jyoti memorial flame at the base of the arch.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the arch, and ask your passer-by to back up along the avenue, a few dozen metres from the gate, so the whole monument fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the paths, as the lawns are largely off limits to walking. Security staff are around, so keep away from sensitive areas. If you're going for the Republic Day parade, check the official site first, because it uses ticketed positions. Smartphones are fine for photos here.
card.challenge: Get the arch dead centre on the gridlines with the avenue leading straight to it, and see if you can keep the crowd down to tiny dots.
card.good_to_know: India Gate was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and stands 42 metres tall on a low base of red Bharatpur stone. It remembers 74,187 Indian soldiers who died between 1914 and 1921, and around 13,300 British Empire servicemen are also named on it. The foundation stone was laid on 10 February 1921, and the arch was inaugurated on 12 February 1931.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Kartavya Path, at the India Gate end of the boulevard. Face east, because the arch is straight along the avenue.

card.hook: Imagine a giant white lotus, half open, with a twin floating upside down in the water at your feet. That's the Lotus Temple, and the pools do half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the edge of the reflecting pools in the temple grounds, right where the phone icon sits at the water's edge. Face the temple and look up at the petal clusters.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, crouching low, to fit the tall petals and their reflection into one frame. Switch to 1x for the full lotus with its mirror image, and try 2x or 5x for the petal edges and marble texture (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest bit of marble, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white petals keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon, when the low sun catches the marble. White stone against almost any sky looks good, but this light is the nicest.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of one of the reflecting pools with the petal clusters rising behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x if you have it so the temple fits over your shoulder. For a different look, try the walkways along the side of the temple, where the petal structure makes a good backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the main entrance on the approach in front of the temple, so the whole lotus and the pools in front of it fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the gardens and outside the building, but not inside the prayer hall. Keep your phone away when you go in and move quietly, as it's a place of worship. Drones are prohibited, so leave yours behind.
card.challenge: Snap the temple and its reflection so the water line sits across the middle of your screen, then see if anyone can tell which half is the real one.
card.good_to_know: The temple was designed by Fariborz Sahba and has 27 petals in three rings of nine. The outer petals are clad in white Pentelic marble from Greece. It stands about 40 metres high and 70 metres across, was dedicated on 24 December 1986 and opened to the public on 1 January 1987.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the edge of the reflecting pools in the temple grounds, right where the phone icon sits at the water's edge. Face the temple and look up at the petal clusters.

card.hook: Imagine two giant stone bowls, with steps wrapped around them and shadows cutting across the markings like someone drew them with a ruler. That's Jantar Mantar, and it's wonderfully photogenic.
card.stand_here: Head for the Jai Prakash Yantra, the pair of bowl-shaped instruments, and stand right at the subject, on the steps around the bowls. Face down into the bowls so you get a slightly raised, top-down view of the markings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both bowls and the steps in. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the markings. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details of the Samrat Yantra's staircase and edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up a curved rim with one of the lines, so the bowls look nicely balanced.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the shadows are long. Some visitors also suggest the east side of the Samrat Yantra for a sunset backdrop and fewer people.
card.selfie_here: Try the east side of the Samrat Yantra, the big triangular sundial. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the sundial over your shoulder. One catch: nobody calls it a selfie spot, so check the landmark really sits behind you before you snap.
card.rules_and_safety: Please stay off the instruments themselves. It's a ticketed monument, so check the official site for entry rules and any photography conditions. Carry water too: there's very little shade past the entrance gate, and the nearest shop is back towards Connaught Place.
card.challenge: Step up a few stairs, then catch a friend (or a stranger!) at the edge of the frame, so the bowls look properly huge.
card.good_to_know: Jantar Mantar is an open-air observatory with 13 large instruments, built for tracking the Sun, Moon and planets by the naked eye. Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur completed it in 1724, and it was the first of his five observatories. The Samrat Yantra stands about 70 feet high and is often called the world's largest sundial.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Jai Prakash Yantra, the pair of bowl-shaped instruments, and stand right at the subject, on the steps around the bowls. Face down into the bowls so you get a slightly raised, top-down view of the markings.

card.hook: Here's a funny thing about one of Delhi's most carved temples: inside, your phone has to stay in a cloakroom. The best photo you can actually take is from a walkover above the highway, with the whole temple glowing across the road.
card.stand_here: Stand on Sunset Point – Akshardham, the elevated walkover on the highway, on the left side when facing the temple. Face south-west and the temple sits right there against the sky above the road. The spot has no official name, so check it on the map before you go.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the temple closer across the road. Then drop to 1x to catch the whole shape with the sky. Use 0.5x only if you want the walkover and traffic in your shot.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the temple on one of the vertical lines and leave lots of sky above it. Then tap the bright sky and slide to darker for a clean silhouette.
card.best_time: Go around sunset, when the temple is either a dark silhouette or lit up against the sky. One guide suggests arriving by about 4:30 PM so you can claim a spot on the walkover before the light changes. After the sun has gone, try night mode and keep your elbows tight against your body.
card.selfie_here: Sunset Point near Akshardham Metro station is a lookout you reach on foot from the metro stop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and see if the temple fits over your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed that exact angle, so have a play and check the result.
card.rules_and_safety: Phones aren't allowed inside the complex and go in the free cloakroom at the entrance. Guides say photography is banned across the whole complex, gardens included, so check the official site before you go. The walkover is a public one outside the temple campus.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the traffic, line the temple up on a gridline, and get the road looking calm and the sky looking dramatic in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Swaminarayan Akshardham opened on 6 November 2005. It's built from Rajasthani pink sandstone and Italian Carrara marble and stands about 43 metres high. It has 234 carved pillars and nine domes, and 148 life-sized elephants ring its base.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Sunset Point – Akshardham, the elevated walkover on the highway, on the left side when facing the temple. Face south-west and the temple sits right there against the sky above the road. The spot has no official name, so check it on the map before you go.

card.hook: Picture a giant white wedding cake of arches wrapped around a park, with a fountain in the middle and you standing in the icing. That's Connaught Place, and it's one of the easiest places in Delhi to look like you know what you're doing with a phone.
card.stand_here: Walk into Central Park at the very centre of the circle and stand near the central fountain. Face outwards so the fountain and gardens are in front of you and the colonnaded buildings sit behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, the gardens and the curve of buildings in one go. Switch to 1x for a tidier shot of just the fountain with the colonnade behind it, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and columns across the park.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain on a lower third with the colonnade across the top, and keep the phone level so the arches don't lean.
card.best_time: Dusk is a good choice, when the buildings are lit and the sky still has some colour. Early morning is quieter if you want fewer people in your photos, and the Inner Circle looks best when the low sun warms the white walls.
card.selfie_here: Try the Inner Circle arcade: stand under the white colonnades with the walkway behind you, using the front camera, and the clean white walls make a bright backdrop. Another option is the circular Rajiv Chowk Metro entrance with the colonnade rising behind you. Switch to 0.5x so more of the buildings fit over your shoulder. Both spots are approximate, so wander a few steps until the arches line up.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photos for your own use are generally fine, but professional shoots may need permission. Ask before photographing shopkeepers or vendors, and before shooting inside shops. Check the official site for any park access rules before you go.
card.challenge: Walk the Inner Circle and get one shot where the colonnade curves away so neatly that your friends ask how many arches there are.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1929 and finished in 1933, designed by Robert Tor Russell. The Georgian look is modelled on the Royal Crescent in Bath. It's named after Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught, and was later renamed Rajiv Chowk, though most people still say Connaught Place.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into Central Park at the very centre of the circle and stand near the central fountain. Face outwards so the fountain and gardens are in front of you and the colonnaded buildings sit behind them.

card.hook: Most people stride straight past the smaller tomb on the way in, heading for the big one. Slow down, because this quiet walled garden is where the stone details are at their best.
card.stand_here: Stand at Isa Khan's Tomb, northwest of the main monument, inside its own walled char bagh enclosure, and face the octagonal sandstone mausoleum. From there the main tomb is roughly 400-450 m to the east, a few minutes' walk (that's a rough estimate).
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the garden and the mosque on the west side. Switch to 1x for the whole mausoleum, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the carved screens and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the octagonal walls straight, then tap the stone wall and slide it a little darker so the pale marble and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before the crowds, when the light on Isa Khan's Tomb and its garden is soft. The light on the main tomb changes through the day, so take a few shots of it at different times if you can.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the edge of the central water channel in the Charbagh garden with the tomb building directly behind you. One guide says the tomb can show up reflected in the water too. For a quick postcard-style selfie, pause at the front entrance arch where the tomb's frontal view opens up. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the tomb over your shoulder.

card.rules_and_safety: This is a ticketed, managed complex, so check the official site before you go for entry rules, opening times and what you can bring. Everyday photography is allowed throughout at no extra charge, but drones are not permitted.

card.good_to_know: Empress Bega Begum paid for Humayun's Tomb, and it was built between 1565 and 1572. It was the first garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. Isa Khan's Tomb is older, built in 1547, about twenty years before the main tomb.

card.hook: Picture a gateway and a row of domes floating above a sea of stalls, signs and people. That's Jama Masjid from the lane out front, and it's very much a working part of Delhi, not a hushed monument.
card.stand_here: Stand on Meena Bazaar, the lane on the east side in front of the east gateway. Face the mosque so the gateway and domes rise above the stalls.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural street view. If the lane is too narrow to fit the gateway and domes, switch to 0.5x. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the domes above the stalls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines so the gateway stands straight, and keep the stalls in the lower part of the frame with the gateway and domes filling the top.
card.best_time: Evening is the one to aim for, when the food stalls are busy and the mosque is lit. Expect the lane to be crowded, so give yourself a moment to find a gap.
card.selfie_here: Try the main eastern entrance staircase, with the mosque's facade behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tilt up a little so the facade fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the courtyard beside gate 1 and shoot toward the prayer hall while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so dress modestly, expect it to close to visitors during prayers, and ask before photographing worshippers. Rules on photography can change, so check the official site before you go. If you climb for a high view, take care: one guide warns the minaret steps are narrow and steep. In the crowded lane, keep checking that your phone is secure.
card.challenge: Can you get the gateway perfectly straight, with a chai stall or two tucked in at the bottom of the frame?
card.good_to_know: Jama Masjid is one of the largest mosques in India, and it still holds regular prayers. Shah Jahan built it at the highest point of his capital, Shahjahanabad (now Old Delhi), and it was inaugurated on 23 July 1656. It served as the emperors' royal mosque until 1857, and its poetic name, Masjid-i-Jehan-Numa, is usually read as 'mosque that reflects the whole world'.

card.hook: Picture a heavy stone gateway sitting on a wide green lawn, with morning walkers drifting past and, on cooler days, mist still hanging in the trees. That's Bara Gumbad, and it's very hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open lawn and path in front of Bara Gumbad and face the main gateway. The square domed gateway and the attached mosque will sit against the park's trees and grass.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the gateway and mosque together. If you're close and the dome is getting chopped off, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the blue tile traces on the Shisha Gumbad.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone wall, then drag the brightness slider down a little (darker) so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the light comes from the east and warms up the stone. From October to February, mist can still be hanging among the trees.
card.selfie_here: Walk in through Gate No. 1 and take your selfie on the open lawn in front of the big dome of Bara Gumbad. Morning light on the stone makes a lovely backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the dome over your shoulder. For a second backdrop, take one on the lawn just opposite, with the Shisha Gumbad behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back toward Gate No. 1 on the walkway while you stand on the lawn path facing Bara Gumbad, so the whole dome and mosque fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are generally fine, but commercial photography or drones may need permission, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for the walkers to pass and grab one shot with nobody in it, then see if you can spot the blue tile left on the Shisha Gumbad.
card.good_to_know: Bara Gumbad means 'big dome'. It isn't a tomb but a gateway, built in 1494 in the reign of Sikandar Lodi, and the three-domed mosque beside it is from the same date. The park's monuments come from the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties, who ruled Delhi from 1414 to 1526, and the Archaeological Survey of India protects the site.

card.hook: Here's the funny thing about this big palace: the long, lawn-lined avenue points straight at it, but the road climbs and the slope hides part of the front. So the dome and upper parts get the starring role.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kartavya Path, on the India Gate side, and face west up the avenue towards Rashtrapati Bhavan. For the full long view, walk further back along Kartavya Path towards India Gate.
card.zoom: From further back, zoom 1x shows the whole avenue leading to the building. Up close the facade fills the frame, so try zoom 0.5x to fit in the lawns and sky, and use zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the dome.

card.rules_and_safety: This is a secured government area, so stay in the public viewing areas and follow staff instructions. Photography is restricted near the gates on Raisina Hill, and permission rules vary, so check before you shoot.

card.good_to_know: Rashtrapati Bhavan is the official residence of the President of India. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed it, and it was built between 1912 and 1929 as the Viceroy's House. With 340 rooms, it is the largest official residence of any head of state in the world by floor area.

card.hook: Most people photograph Bangla Sahib across the water, but the front gate on Ashoka Road is a calm, tidy shot that most people skip. The gate is a strong, simple shape, and the golden dome and flagpole above it give your picture a clear centre.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ashoka Road on the main gate side, about 69 m south-west of the middle of the complex, and face north-east toward the gate. It's an approximate spot, so shuffle a few steps along the pavement until the gate sits clear of poles and vehicles.

card.good_to_know: Bangla Sahib began as the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh I of Amber, where the eighth Sikh Guru, Guru Har Krishan, stayed during his time in Delhi. That's where the word 'bangla' comes from. It was rebuilt as a small shrine in 1783 by the Sikh general Sardar Baghel Singh, and the holy pool, the Sarovar, measures 225 by 235 feet.

card.hook: Three spires, white marble and red sandstone, and a strip of garden at the bottom: Birla Mandir is a lot of temple for one photo. Luckily, there's one spot on the street where it all fits.
card.stand_here: Stand on Mandir Marg, opposite the temple's main front, and face east toward the entrance. From here you get the whole three-spired front with the garden greenery below it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the full front. If the pavement is crowded or you're close, drop to 0.5x. Use zoom 2x to home in on the spires.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white marble, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the stone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Come in the late afternoon or evening, when the marble is said to turn a warm gold.
card.selfie_here: Head into the landscaped garden near the fountains and animal sculptures, where guides say photos are fine. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want more in, and let the three spires sit behind you across the garden. The rock-built artificial hill with its waterfall on the garden paths is another popular place to pose.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo at the stone chariot of Krishna and Arjuna in the area behind the temple, with you standing beside the chariot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed inside the temple building, but exterior and garden photos are fine. One guide says phones must go in the free lockers at the entrance gate, so check the signs there before you head in.
card.challenge: Line the middle spire up with a gridline, then find a fountain for your second shot and see if you can get both in the same photo.
card.good_to_know: Birla Mandir is a Hindu temple to Lakshmi and Vishnu, built between 1933 and 1939 by the industrialist Jugal Kishore Birla. Mahatma Gandhi opened it on the condition that people of all castes could enter. The tallest spire is about 49 m, and the whole complex covers roughly 3 hectares.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Mandir Marg, opposite the temple's main front, and face east toward the entrance. From here you get the whole three-spired front with the garden greenery below it.

card.hook: Most people march straight to the black marble platform, but the calmer picture is waiting in the gardens next door. Think long lines of trees, quiet lawns and a river nearby.
card.stand_here: Stand in Shanti Van, the tree-lined memorial gardens just north of Raj Ghat, and face along the lawns and rows of trees. Raj Ghat's platform is about 1 km to the south, but don't count on seeing it from here, so treat this as a garden and atmosphere shot.

card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules can vary, so check on the day and look at the official site for current rules and timings. Keep your phone low-key, don't photograph people who are praying, and don't fly a drone, as they are prohibited. Carry water and sun protection, because Delhi's heat can be intense, especially from April to June.

card.good_to_know: Raj Ghat is where Mahatma Gandhi was cremated on 31 January 1948. His memorial is a plain black marble platform with an eternal flame at one end. The name loosely means 'Royal Steps', after the steps that once led up from the Yamuna river, and the complex has since grown to include memorials to other national leaders.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Shanti Van, the tree-lined memorial gardens just north of Raj Ghat, and face along the lawns and rows of trees. Raj Ghat's platform is about 1 km to the south, but don't count on seeing it from here, so treat this as a garden and atmosphere shot.

card.hook: Right in the middle of busy central Delhi, 108 stone steps drop away between thick walls, and suddenly the traffic noise fades. Everything here repeats, so even a quick snap looks tidy.
card.stand_here: Head to Agrasen ki Baoli on Hailey Road, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the stepwell. For the quieter shot, walk down to a lower level, turn round and face back up towards the open sky.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole staircase in. Switch to 1x for the shot looking up, and if your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for arches and people further away.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the walls up on either side, so the shot looks balanced and the steps pull the eye in.
card.best_time: Go when the stepwell is open and fairly quiet, because the steps are much easier to photograph without crowds. Bright daylight gives you the strongest contrast between the dark walls and the sky.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the first step at the top landing with the steps filling the frame behind you, using the front camera at 0.5x to show the whole stepwell. For a close-up, sit inside one of the arched alcoves along the stairs and let the stone arch frame you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the top landing and ask your helper to wait three to four levels down the main staircase, so the walls show how deep the place goes.
card.rules_and_safety: Phone and personal photography is allowed, but commercial shoots need permission and drones are not allowed. It's a protected monument, so opening times and restrictions can change; check the official site before you go. Watch your step on the stairs and don't lean over edges for a selfie.
card.challenge: Find a bright rectangle of sky framed by dark stone, then get a friend or an arch to make a perfect silhouette in it.
card.good_to_know: The stepwell is about 60 metres long and 15 metres wide. Nobody knows for certain who built it, but tradition says the Aggarwal community built it in the name of their ancestor Agrasen, and the architecture suggests a 14th-century rebuild, probably Tughlaq or Lodi. It has also appeared in several Bollywood films, so the view may look familiar.

card.hook: Picture a huge red wall rising straight out of a quiet lake, with a few trees leaning in like they're photobombing. The fort is just under a kilometre across, so don't try to fit it all in. Pick one view and make it a good one.
card.stand_here: Head to Old Fort Lake, on the lake shore below the walls and outside the main gate. The fort lies to the east of you, so face east with the water in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the full wall and its reflection. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the battlements and gateway details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water along the lower third line, and tap the brightest part of the wall, then drag the slider a touch darker so the red stone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when travel guides say the light on the water works best. On a windless morning, try a Live Photo and pick the stillest frame for the reflection.
card.selfie_here: At the lake edge, turn your back to the fort walls and use the front camera, with the walls rising over your shoulder. For a second selfie, stand just outside the arch of the main western gate, Bara Darwaza, with the gate behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lake edge facing the fort across the water, so the walls and gates fit in the frame with you in it.
card.rules_and_safety: The lake-side viewpoint is listed as free, but entry to the fort and its museum may be ticketed or restricted, and photos are limited inside the museum, so check the official site first. The stone surfaces, especially the steps up to Sher Mandal, need steady footing, so wear comfortable shoes.
card.challenge: Turn your phone to landscape and give the wall the top half of the frame and the water the bottom half, with a little tree or grass tucked in at the edge.
card.good_to_know: Purana Qila, the Old Fort, is one of the oldest forts in Delhi. The present fort is attributed to Humayun and Sher Shah Suri, though that's disputed, and it once formed the inner citadel of the city of Dinpanah. Until the early 20th century it was still called Pandavon Ka Qila, because it was linked with the ancient city of Indraprastha.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Old Fort Lake, on the lake shore below the walls and outside the main gate. The fort lies to the east of you, so face east with the water in front.

card.hook: Most people snap Safdarjung's Tomb straight on from the gate and move on. Walk into the garden to the quiet pavilion on the north side instead, and the arches frame the whole tomb for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at Moti Mahal, the pavilion on the north side of the garden. The tomb is to the south, about 2 minutes on foot, so face south and look through the arches.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If the arches are too close to fit the whole tomb, try zoom 0.5x. Use zoom 2x for a tighter shot of the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the arch and tomb upright, then tap the tomb and slide it a little darker so the bright stone isn't washed out by the shaded arch.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the red-and-buff stone. For the back of the tomb, try softer evening light. Opening times can vary, so check the official site on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawn beside the fountain and water channel in the garden. Use the front camera and turn so the dome rises behind the pond over your shoulder. Go wider with zoom 0.5x if your front camera has it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the central arch of the entrance gate while you stand on the central pathway, so they can catch you with the tomb behind.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the garden and around the outside of the tomb, but not inside the main chamber where the cenotaphs are. Skip sitting under the trees because of the insects. The green ground away from them or the benches are better.
card.challenge: Get the whole tomb sitting neatly in the arch, with both arch edges showing and nobody wandering through. Patience counts as a skill here.
card.good_to_know: Safdarjung's Tomb was built in 1754 for Safdarjung, Nawab of Awadh and prime minister of the Mughal Empire. It is often called the last great garden tomb of the Mughals. It uses the same char bagh plan as Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal, with the tomb at the centre of a walled garden split into four squares.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Moti Mahal, the pavilion on the north side of the garden. The tomb is to the south, about 2 minutes on foot, so face south and look through the arches.

card.hook: Here's a fun puzzle: one Parliament, two buildings, and one of them is a triangle. Vijay Chowk gives you the wide open space to fit the grand scene in without bumping into anyone's elbow.
card.stand_here: Stand in Vijay Chowk, the open plaza where Rajpath meets Sansad Marg. The new Parliament House is about 190 m to the north-east, so face that way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the building and its surroundings in one frame. Zoom 2x to 5x picks out details without you walking closer, and zoom 0.5x is for fitting the whole plaza and the Secretariat blocks in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings level, then tap the building and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the stone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the plaza. It's worth checking how busy the area is on the day.
card.selfie_here: Vijay Chowk is a good place to try one, since the square is where the Parliament building comes into view. Use the front camera (or zoom 0.5x if you can) and keep the building over your shoulder. Rajpath near the India Gate end, facing back toward the building, is a second spot to try.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Sansad Marg, the wide road crossing Rajpath at Vijay Chowk, where the building comes into the frame on the left as you head toward India Gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the building or the museum, and access around the complex is restricted. Stay on public roads and footpaths, and follow any instructions from security staff.
card.challenge: Get the plaza filling the bottom of your frame, a straight horizon, and a North or South Block sneaking into the shot. That's three grand things in one photo.
card.good_to_know: The older circular sandstone building opened in January 1927 and was designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. The new triangular building, just to its east, has four floors, matches the old one's height and was inaugurated on 28 May 2023. On its roof sits a cast sculpture of the national emblem, 6.5 m high.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Vijay Chowk, the open plaza where Rajpath meets Sansad Marg. The new Parliament House is about 190 m to the north-east, so face that way.
